items.title: ARMS 2026: UTS TeamBuilder: AI and data driven insights for building cross-university collaboration
items.abstract: Universities have a wide range of expertise, but identifying the right people for complex, cross-disciplinary opportunities can be difficult. Expertise is often spread across faculties, research centres and different institutional systems. When funding and partnership opportunities have short response periods, those supporting team formation may rely on familiar networks and people with relevant but less obvious capabilities. UTS TeamBuilder is an AI-assisted tool that helps people find the right researchers, explore expertise across the university, and form teams around new opportunities. Rather than simply producing a list of names, the tool supports the broader team formation process, from framing the challenge and exploring institutional capability to preparing introductions and facilitating early conversations. The tool brings together evidence from multiple institutional sources, including researcher profiles, publication abstracts, research projects, proposals and staff bios. It uses natural language processing, network analysis, interactive visualization and generative AI to help users explore expertise, assess possible team combinations, and understand the evidence behind suggestions. Outputs can include expertise landscapes, preliminary team propositions, personalised invitations and prompts to support early team conversations. A key principle behind the tool is that AI should support, rather than replace, human judgement. Users can inspect the visualizations and analysis used by the AI, refine the researcher pool, explore proposed team members, and adjust the direction of the analysis. TeamBuilder therefore broadens the user’s field of view and provides informed starting points, while leaving decisions about team composition and suitability with the human user.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Indian Labour Market: A Comprehensive Analysis of Employment Effects, Channels and Distributional Effects
items.abstract: Abstract: AI is flooding into India's job market faster than most legislative frameworks can keep up with. This review draws together nineteen peer-reviewed publications, working papers and institutional reports, mostly published between 2023 and 2026, in order to evaluate what is empirically known about the employment effects of AI in India, as opposed to what is anticipated or assumed. The review finds that empirical evidence is still concentrated in India's formal services sector, where AI-related hiring has skyrocketed since 2016 and appears to have reduced demand for high-skilled managerial and analytical roles rather than low-skilled ones. Most of the Indian workers are engaged in manufacturing, agriculture and the informal economy, all of which have little evidence largely based on projections and not empirical. The review categorises the literature based on four recurring mechanisms: task displacement, task reinstatement, productivity-driven labour demand and skill polarisation. Distributional data show AI exposure in India is stratified by caste, gender and educational attainment. The most urgent void in Indian literature is sector-specific, worker-level empirical research outside of IT services. items.title: Artificial Intelligence Applications in Power Systems: A Review of Methods, Use Cases, and Future Directions
items.abstract: Modern electrical networks face growing operational demands as electricity consumption rises and renewable generation, distributed resources, and electric vehicles become more common. Artificial intelligence (AI) can learn useful relationships from operating records and simulated data, supporting tasks such as demand prediction, fault identification, state estimation, stability screening, and energy scheduling. This review organizes reported AI techniques and applications in both large interconnected grids and smaller power systems. It considers rule-based and fuzzy approaches alongside machine learning, deep learning, reinforcement learning, and newer foundation-model methods. The literature suggests that AI may accelerate selected analyses and provide flexible decision support, but dependable performance still relies on representative data, generalization, explainability, cyber protection, and real-world validation. A staged approach that combines AI with engineering models and expert oversight is outlined. This paper synthesizes existing studies and does not claim new experimental results..

items.title: Artificial Intelligence as an Assistant in Research Evaluation and Peer Review: A Critical Case for Augmentation Without Replacement
items.abstract: Peer review is important in maintaining the quality of scholarly publishing, but the process faces challenges such as shortage of reviewers, delays, inconsistent judgements, and overlooked errors. These challenges have increased the need to consider the appropriate use of artificial intelligence (AI) in peer review. Completely excluding AI or allowing it to function as an autonomous reviewer may not adequately address these problems. A Human–AI Augmented Review model is therefore proposed, in which AI supports clearly defined tasks under human supervision, while reviewers and editors retain responsibility for interpretation, ethical judgement, and editorial decisions. Peer review involves both routine technical checks and complex scholarly evaluation. AI can assist with repetitive and rule-based tasks such as manuscript screening, consistency checking, reviewer identification, and identification of reporting gaps. Human reviewers are still needed to assess methodology, scholarly contribution, and ethical issues. Effective use of AI requires a clear division of responsibilities, verification points within the review process, and governance measures to address bias, hallucinations, confidentiality, and excessive reliance on automation. Careful and limited use of AI can improve efficiency and reduce avoidable errors while maintaining accountability and trust in peer review.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Attitudes and Readiness Among Undergraduate Nursing Students: A Cross-Sectional Study
items.abstract: Purpose:This study examined undergraduate nursing students’ attitudes toward artificial intelligence and their readiness for medical artificial intelligence, as well as the factors associated with AI readiness.Methods: A descriptive, cross-sectional design was employed. Two hundred and fifty undergraduate nursing students at a nursing faculty in western Türkiye participated during the 2025–2026 academic year. Three instruments were administered: a Participant Information Form, the General Attitudes toward Artificial Intelligence Scale, and the Medical Artificial Intelligence Readiness Scale for Medical Students.Results: The Positive General Attitudes toward Artificial Intelligence Scale yielded a mean of 3.88 ± 0.66, the Negative General Attitudes toward Artificial Intelligence Scale 3.26 ± 0.87, and the Medical Artificial Intelligence Readiness Scale for Medical Students 74.29 ± 13.43. Academic year was significantly associated with AI readiness. One-way ANOVA showed significant differences across year groups (F = 3.450; p = 0.012; η² = 0.040), with fourth-year students scoring higher than second-year students. In the multiple linear regression analysis, both second-year (β = −0.156, p = 0.014) and third-year (β = −0.143, p = 0.024) students had significantly lower readiness scores compared with fourth-year students. A moderate positive correlation was observed between positive AI attitudes and readiness scores(r = 0.430; p < 0.01). Positive attitudes toward AI and self-reported computer skills emerged as the strongest independent factors associated with readiness.Conclusion: Nursing students displayed generally favorable attitudes toward AI, yet readiness levels varied across academic years. Attitude and readiness, while correlated, appear to be distinct constructs. These findings highlight the need for intentional, practice-oriented integration of AI competencies into undergraduate nursing curricula.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Cyber Defense: From Intelligent Threat Detection to Autonomous AI Agents
items.abstract: The article provides a comprehensive analysis of the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in cybersecurity, taking into account the latest technological trends of 2024–2026. The main possibilities of applying AI to protect information systems are studied: automatic detection of threats and anomalies, real-time incident response, prediction and prevention of cyberattacks, recognition of malicious code and phishing, and continuous learning and adaptation of defense systems. Particular attention is paid to the phenomenon of autonomous AI agents as a new stage in the evolution of intelligent cyber defense systems: practical cases of agentic incident triage and investigation systems (Microsoft Security Copilot), autonomous vulnerability discovery (Google Big Sleep), autonomous penetration testing (XBOW, PentestGPT), as well as the first documented case of an AI-orchestrated cyber espionage campaign are analyzed. The risks and challenges associated with the use of AI are considered: misuse of technologies by attackers, false positives and missed threats, vulnerabilities of machine learning models and agentic systems, and ethical and legal aspects. The necessity of a balanced approach combining automated AI systems with expert human control based on human-in-the-loop and human-on-the-loop models is substantiated.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Medical Education: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning, natural language processing, and generative AI, is rapidly transforming medical education, particularly anatomy, assessment, and simulation.Objective: To systematically review the applications, educational benefits, limitations, ethical concerns, and emerging trends of AI in medical education since 2023.Methods: A structured literature search was conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, and major medical-education publishers for studies published from January 2023 to July 2026.Twenty-nine eligible studies were synthesised across seven thematic domains.Results: AI applications included large language models, anatomy education tools, virtual simulation, AI-assisted assessment, and personalised learning.Evidence suggests potential benefits in learning support, simulation, question generation, and anatomy education.However, concerns regarding accuracy, hallucination, bias, academic integrity, privacy, and inadequate AI literacy remain.Evidence for improved educational outcomes is still limited, with many studies being small, single-centre, or pilot investigations.Conclusion: AI is becoming an important component of medical education, with particularly promising applications in anatomy and pre-clinical teaching.Responsible integration requires faculty oversight, competency-based AI literacy, ethical governance, validation of AI-generated educational content, and stronger outcome-based research.

items.title: Artificial Obedience: How Large Language Models (LLMs) May Normalize Hierarchical Communication
items.abstract: This study introduces the concept of computer communication spillover: the transfer of interaction patterns from human–computer to human–human contexts via cue-triggered habit activation. The possibility of such transfer is supported by theories of power, habit formation, and social practice. Human interaction with large language models (LLMs) is here presented as a theoretical example, where the compliant nature of LLMs is central to the argument. We argue that by repeatedly occupying a superior, controlling position, LLM users may develop directive, instrumental, and control-oriented communication habits. Such habits might spill over to human-human communication contexts, where they could reduce politeness, tolerance for dissent, and openness to other people' perspectives. Because habits typically develop gradually, outside users’ awareness, spillover effects can raise ethical-legal questions about responsibility and human agency. Overall, we propose that computer communication spillover might be a broader societal risk of generative AI.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: Assertion without a Speaker: Testimony, Tracking, and Large Language Models
items.abstract: Abstract Large language models produce assertion-shaped outputs that often bring their users to true belief. I argue for two conclusions of different strengths: that on the best current evidence, these systems do not transmit testimonial knowledge and that hearers are not now positioned to accord their outputs testimonial uptake, which does not wait on the first. From Burge, Williamson, Goldberg, Faulkner, and Lackey, I derive a Tracking Minimum: a source transmits testimonial knowledge that p only if the truth of p , or the evidential support for p , figures in the explanation of its producing that assertion, and does so in virtue of the source’s own production process rather than of a proxy on which that process depends. It is this endogeneity requirement, not any modal profile, that the five accounts share and current systems fail. The argument engages Burge’s extension of his framework to computational sources, the interpretability literature, and the published case for AI testimony, whose dispute with mine turns on an empirically decidable question, for which an experiment is specified. The positive proposal places LLM outputs within an extended epistemology of instruments, with a result that has gone unremarked: a working barometer satisfies the condition these systems fail.

items.title: Autonomous Agents Based on Large Language Models: Reasoning Strategies and Multi-Agent Interaction
items.abstract: Language-model agents acquire capability along two routes that published work almost always varies together, one enlarging the computation a single agent performs and the other enlarging the number of agents and the channels along which they pass partial results, which leaves the contribution of each route indistinguishable. This paper separates an agent system into a reasoning operator and an interaction topology, holding the number of agents fixed at three across all multi-agent topologies, together with the number of rounds, the message cap, the prompt skeleton, and the memory settings for all combinations, and evaluates a full factorial design of four reasoning levels and four topologies on three public test sets totalling 484 instances under five random seeds, giving 38,720 task executions. Comparisons are paired at the instance level, and effects are estimated from logistic mixed-effects models fitted to each test set separately. The reasoning factor spans 18.0 points on the static suite whereas the topology factor spans 7.8 points on the interactive one, a reversal indicating that the two mechanisms act on different failure modes. The topology span is taken across all four topology levels and therefore includes the step from one agent to three, against a structure-only span of 2.8 points among the multi-agent topologies. The two factors also depart from additivity in a localised manner. A mechanism-motivated single-degree-of-freedom contrast on the only cell in which both factors contribute a corrective pass is significant at p = 0.001 on the static suite, whereas the omnibus nine-degree-of-freedom interaction test is not (p = 0.094), and in that cell the observed 50.0 percent lies 5.8 points below the additive expectation. After tokens are counted, seven of the sixteen configurations remain undominated on the static suite and five on the operating-system suite, and returns saturate at 12,400 tokens per instance on the static suite under the present design.

items.title: Beyond Correctness: How Novice Software Engineering Students Exercise Oversight of Generative AI
items.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is shifting software engineering students' work from producing artefacts towards evaluating and supervising AI-generated outputs. However, little is known about what characteristics students identify in outputs when reporting interventions, or how they exercise oversight during authentic software engineering work. We analysed 962 student-AI interaction turns documented by 145 first-year software engineering students through structured AI Journals, including 172 student-declared interventions. Using a multi-dimensional coding framework, we characterised the output characteristics identified in these reported interventions, students' reasons for intervening, the actions they took, and how those actions were enacted. Fitness problems were identified in 74.4% of interventions, compared with 16.9% involving correctness problems, indicating that oversight more often concerned whether plausible AI outputs were suitable for the engineering task than whether they contained explicit errors. Among classifiable interventions, students most frequently modified generated outputs (51.0%) or refined their prompts (28.2%), with both response types commonly associated with engineering fit. Within-student analysis further showed that outputs perceived as containing minor flaws were associated with lower evaluation confidence than outputs perceived as perfect. Taken together, these findings characterise novice AI oversight as a process that extends beyond error detection to encompass both judgement of fitness for purpose and active intervention in AI-assisted engineering work.

items.title: BEYOND TECHNOSTRESS AI Fatigue as a Cumulative Adaptation Burden in Education and Work
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence has become a persistent layer of work and learning rather than an occasional tool. Users must repeatedly decide when to delegate, how to prompt, whether to trust, how to verify, and how responsibility should be distributed. This integrative review defines AI fatigue as a cumulative reduction in the cognitive, affective, or motivational capacity for adaptive AI engagement when interaction, evaluation, correction, learning, and role-adjustment demands accumulate faster than recovery and support. The review connects technostress, automation vigilance, cognitive load and offloading, trust calibration, digital fatigue, and the Job Demands–Resources perspective. It introduces an Exposure–Adaptation–Depletion–Response framework, a five-domain taxonomy, and an AI Fatigue Load model that separates use volume from uncertainty, task stakes, correction burden, interruption, role disruption, and imposed adoption velocity. The analysis is updated to incorporate a 2026 validated 15-item AI Fatigue Scale; the proposed load model complements that psychophysiological outcome measure by specifying socio-technical antecedents and exposure conditions. Educational and organizational applications show why AI may simultaneously improve output and worsen human sustainability. The article identifies recurring inferential errors, presents a measurement and longitudinal research agenda, and proposes an intervention hierarchy spanning interface design, workflow, curriculum, organizational policy, and governance. AI fatigue is positioned neither as generic screen tiredness nor as a synonym for burnout, but as an adaptation problem located in the coupled human–AI–institution system.

items.title: BEYOND THE CLASSROOM: ANALYZING THE FACTORS AFFECTING GRADE 12 LEARNERS’ COLLEGE COURSE PREFERENCES
items.abstract: This study utilized a quantitative descriptive-survey and correlational-predictive research design to systematically examine the variables dictating the college preferences of graduating senior high school learners. Conducted at Mindanao State University - Lanao National College of Arts and Trades (MSU-LNCAT) during the School Year 2025–2026, the investigation relied on a total seventy-three Grade 12 learner-respondents comprising of forty-three Humanities and Social Sciences Learner-respondents (58.90%) and thirty TVL track learner-respondents (41.10%), with a demographic concentration of fifty-six females (76.71%) and seventeen males (23.29%). Data was gathered via face-to-face classroom administration using a structured 5-point Likert scale questionnaire evaluating three predictive dimensions: Intrinsic Motivation, Familial Influence, and Peer Dynamics and Social Media Influence. Descriptive and inferential statistical treatments was used including frequency, percentage, weighted mean, standard deviation, item ranking, and the Pearson (r) Correlation Coefficient. Intrinsic Motivation emerged as the primary driver, yielding a high composite mean of 3.92 (High Influence) and a Significant Strong Positive Relationship, with course preferences, successfully rejecting the null hypothesis. Conversely, external factors had minimal impact; Familial Influence acted strictly as a secondary, consultative reference point with a neutral composite mean of 3.39 (Moderate Influence) and a weak, variable correlation, while Peer Dynamics and Social Media Influence exerted the weakest pressure, finishing with a low composite mean of 2.68 (Low Influence) and No Significant Relationship. Ultimately, these findings demonstrate that modern Grade 12 learner-respondents at MSU-LNCAT exercise high psychological autonomy, systematically prioritizing internal passion and specialized tracking competencies over parental expectations, peer circles, or digital trends.

items.title: Beyond What to Say: Proactive Utterance Timing with Inner Thoughts for Werewolf Agents
items.abstract: Participating in a conversation involves not only deciding what to say but also whether to speak at all. This judgment carries even greater significance in environments like the Werewolf game, where participants' interests conflict, because both utterances and silence are subject to interpretation and assessment by others. Therefore, determining when to speak, as well as what to say, is crucial for an LLM agent playing the Werewolf game. In this study, we introduce a Werewolf AI agent developed for the Anytime Utterance Track of the AIWolfDial shared task. Our system builds on the existing Inner Thoughts framework, which determines utterance timing during conversations by generating internal thoughts and evaluating the value of each thought for expression at that moment. Since existing methods were designed for general dialogue, we have redesigned the system specifically for the competitive environment and incomplete information setting of Werewolf games. We call our adapted method Adversarial Inner Thoughts. Through experiments involving analysis of self-play logs and human evaluations, we analyze and discuss the effectiveness of our approach.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

items.title: Can AI Agents Help Robotic Engineers? Lessons from Two Focus Days in Industry
items.abstract: Software developers increasingly use AI agents that execute multi-step programming tasks on their own. However, it is unclear if and how this transfers to robotic engineering, where engineers program industrial robots in niche, vendor-specific languages and rely on visual feedback from simulation tools. Within this paper, we report a case study on the use of AI agents by an SME that programs industrial robots. Our results show that the agent did not make the engineers more productive, with the exception of a task that required the generation of highly repetitive code. However, the results with the agent improved over time, as the engineers learned how to use it and the agent was adapted to the domain. Moreover, the experience with AI mattered more for the success with the agent than the experience with robotic engineering. This shows that AI agents are not a plug-and-play solution. Instead, companies must train their engineers on the usage of agents, plan time for a learning curve, and ensure that agent configurations match the domain and developer requirements. The strong learning curve we observed further implies that studies on productivity gains with AI should be longitudinal, as they otherwise miss how engineers adopt agents in practice.

items.title: Can education set the agenda for AI? Simulated innovation and pedagogical direction-setting in teacher education
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) creates a critical inflection point in the relationship between educational innovation and technological development. For decades, educational systems have often been positioned reactively: technologies emerge, institutions search for their possible pedagogical uses, and teacher education programmes adapt belatedly to tools designed elsewhere. This article argues that GenAI makes this sequence increasingly insufficient. Because GenAI can produce texts, explanations, feedback, learning resources, and assessment artefacts that resemble evidence of educational performance, it compels education to define more clearly what should count as learning, authorship, judgement, and valid evidence. The article develops the concept of simulated innovation to describe technology-led change that signals modernisation without transforming pedagogical purposes, assessment logics, teacher judgement, student agency, or learning relationships. It then argues that GenAI opens the possibility of pedagogical direction-setting: beginning from educational, ethical, epistemic, and democratic aims, and requiring technology to respond to those aims. Teacher education is positioned as a strategic site for this shift, not because teachers alone can govern AI-mediated education, but because professional formation can prepare educators to translate pedagogical purposes into criteria for design, assessment, ethical judgement, and technology governance.

items.title: Changes in the acceptance of artificial intelligence in medicine among physicians and the general public in Japan: A repeated cross-sectional comparison of 2018 and 2025
items.abstract: Medical artificial intelligence (AI) has advanced rapidly, yet whether growing societal familiarity with AI is accompanied by greater willingness to receive relatively autonomous AI-led care remains unclear. We conducted repeated cross-sectional online surveys in Japan in 2018 and 2025 using the same questionnaire and compared self-identified physicians and members of the general public (2018: 399 physicians and 600 members of the public; 2025: 300 physicians and 300 members of the public). Mean responses to the item assessing intention to use medical AI did not differ significantly between survey years in either group, despite consistently favorable evaluations of its usefulness and future necessity. Among physicians, the unadjusted mean response regarding the potential of medical AI to improve clinical efficiency was higher in 2025, but this difference was not significant after adjustment for age and sex. Among members of the public, self-rated knowledge of medical AI was higher in 2025, while expectations that medical AI would increase healthcare costs were also greater. These findings suggest that increased self-rated knowledge may not necessarily be accompanied by greater intention to use relatively autonomous medical AI. Implementation strategies should therefore address concerns regarding responsibility, safety, data protection, and healthcare costs alongside efforts to improve public understanding.

items.title: Constructing a Generative AI Framework for Personalised Instructional Resource Development: A Quasi-Experimental Evaluation in a Micro-Lecture Design and Production Course
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is promoted as a way of tailoring instruction to learners, yet most reported applications stay within language and general-education settings, and few measure outcomes in courses whose value lies in design and production skill. This paper describes a four-module generative AI framework for resource development that links learner and content modelling, generation, assessment and community iteration to a course-grounded knowledge base, with the teacher reviewing before release. It was evaluated in a twelve-week quasi-experiment in a professional core course, Micro-lecture Design and Production, at a Chinese vocational college. Two intact classes (n = 45, 44) were taught by the same instructor, who designed the framework; assignment was not random. Covariance-adjusted posttest means differed by 5.6 points (82.3 versus 76.7, p < .001, partial η² = .24), and the framework-supported class reported higher motivation and satisfaction; self-directed learning differed modestly. Preparation time per unit fell by half, though the work became more concentrated and the knowledge base carried a large one-off cost. Because the design cannot separate the framework from the additional resources it produced, the results are framed as associations rather than effects.

items.title: Conversational AI in Digital Marketing: Human-Like Interaction, Perceived Empathy, and Customer Loyalty
items.abstract: This study examined associations among Human-Like Interaction, Perceived Empathy, and Customer Loyalty in the use of conversational artificial intelligence (AI) for Indonesian e-commerce. A cross-sectional survey collected questionnaire responses from 300 purposively selected consumers who had experience with e-commerce chatbots or virtual assistants. The analysis used partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4 to assess 18 indicators across three reflective constructs. The reported measurement properties met the specified reliability and validity thresholds. The reported PLS-SEM results indicated positive direct associations among Human-Like Interaction, Perceived Empathy, and Customer Loyalty, alongside a positive specific indirect association through Perceived Empathy. However, discrepancies between the structural model and the direct-effects table prevent a definitive interpretation of the estimated effect magnitudes and mediation type. However, coefficients in the structural diagram differed from those in the direct-effects table, so the magnitudes and type of mediation could not be confirmed from the reported outputs. The study distinguishes perceived conversational naturalness from perceived understanding and company-directed loyalty intentions. These findings concern self-reported perceptions and intentions rather than observed repurchase behavior. Its cross-sectional design and purposive sample preclude causal conclusions and population-wide generalization. The results provide a basis for evaluating interaction quality and perceived understanding in chatbot-supported customer service.

items.title: Crowd Discrimination in the Digital Workplace: How AI and Platforms Translate Public Bias into Employment Practices
items.abstract: In today's digital workplace, employment decisions are increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence (AI) and social media platforms, embedding societal biases into managerial practices and undermining traditional legal safeguards. This article introduces the concept of crowd discrimination, which arises when biases originating from customers, algorithms, or online communities influence employment outcomes, thus threatening workers' right to equality. Specifically, it argues that platform-based work, AI-driven management tools, and online shaming systematically transform crowd biases into employment decisions regarding hiring, dismissal, wages, and working conditions. Crowd discrimination is not incidental. It results from both technological design and the limitations of existing laws, which fail to adequately address these new discriminatory practices. Employers utilize AI and platform infrastructures, whether intentionally or not, to distance their decisions from discriminatory effects, thereby evading legal accountability. Meanwhile, platform and AI companies shape employment conditions through their technologies without recognized legal responsibility, complicating employers' obligations under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act and obscuring the sources of discrimination. To address these challenges, the article calls for new legal duties to protect workplace equality. It proposes procedural protections enabling workers to enforce equality rights, particularly in cases mediated by AI systems and platforms. Further, it argues for imposing direct liability on platform and AI companies whose technologies facilitate discrimination, whether through embedding biased patterns into AI tools or allowing customer preferences to dictate employment outcomes. By adopting this broader legal approach, the article offers a comprehensive framework to address the threats crowd discrimination poses to workplace equality.

items.title: DEVELOPING TEACHERS' PROFESSIONAL-DEONTOLOGICAL COMPETENCE IN THE AGE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE: ETHICAL RESPONSIBILITY, PEDAGOGICAL JUDGMENT, AND PROFESSIONAL AGENCY
items.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI), digital learning environments, and data-driven educational technologies is transforming the professional responsibilities of teachers and creating new demands for ethical and pedagogical decision-making. This paper examines the theoretical foundations of developing teachers’ professional-deontological competence in the context of digital transformation. The study aims to conceptualize professional-deontological competence as an integrated capacity encompassing ethical knowledge, professional responsibility, pedagogical judgment, digital ethics, and reflective practice. A conceptual and analytical approach is employed to examine relevant philosophical perspectives, contemporary teacher competency frameworks, and emerging challenges associated with AI-supported education. The analysis identifies five interrelated dimensions of professional-deontological competence: ethical and normative awareness, value-based professional commitment, responsible pedagogical decision-making, digital and AI ethics, and reflective professional development. The paper argues that effective teacher education should move beyond the transmission of professional codes toward the systematic integration of ethical reasoning into authentic pedagogical situations. It proposes a conceptual framework combining case-based learning, ethical dilemma analysis, reflective practice, and responsible AI use. The paper concludes that strengthening professional-deontological competence is essential for preserving teacher agency, protecting learners’ dignity, and ensuring that technological innovation remains consistent with the humanistic purposes of education. The proposed framework requires further empirical investigation to establish its effectiveness across different educational contexts.

items.title: Development and exploratory validation of the student susceptibility to artificial intelligence (SAI) index among higher education students in Ghana
items.abstract: Abstract Background Generative AI is now routine in student work, yet instruments measuring the risks attached to that use—over-reliance, misuse, and the reflective practices that guard against them—remain scarce in African higher education. This study reports the initial development and exploratory evaluation of a 23-item Student Susceptibility to AI (SAI) item pool. Methods A cross-sectional survey of 408 students, recruited by convenience sampling at six purposively selected Ghanaian institutions, was analysed using a reverse-coding audit, Principal Axis Factoring with Promax rotation, parallel analysis, false-discovery-rate-corrected comparisons and multivariable regression. No pilot preceded the survey, and one sample informed item evaluation and extraction. Results Two-thirds of participants (65.7%) reported daily AI use; only 2.0% none. Parallel analysis supported three factors, the fourth eigenvalue falling below the random threshold; both solutions are reported. Internal consistency was acceptable for Over-Reliance, Cognitive Vulnerability and Resilience & Reflection (α = 0.807–0.824) but inadequate for Misuse/Academic Integrity (α = 0.535), and a total composite was unsupported (ECV = 0.373). Use frequency produced the largest group differences of any variable examined, though adjusted predictors explained only 2.7–7.9% of variance. Conclusion AI use is already near-universal here, so the question is not whether students use these tools but how. Reflective verification practices proved largely independent of the risk dimensions, indicating that susceptibility is not simply a function of use intensity: interventions should target how students interrogate AI output, not how often they consult it. The item pool remains promising but unstable, requiring revision and independent confirmation.

items.title: Development and Validation of the Manual Integrated Ergonomics Risk Assessment Tool (MIERAT): Field Application in a Small-Scale Automotive Service Environment
items.abstract: Work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WRMSDs) remain a major occupational health challenge, and automotive service work is a high-risk context involving awkward postures, repetitive tasks, and sustained static loading. Conventional ergonomic tools capture static posture snapshots and do not reflect how musculoskeletal stress accumulates over time. This study developed the Manual Integrated Ergonomics Risk Assessment Tool (MIERAT), a low-cost, observation-based framework for resource-constrained automotive settings, and conducted an initial field validation. MIERAT combines REBA-based posture severity (PS), exposure duration (D), and a calibrated Time Modifier (TM; 1.0–2.5) into a Cumulative Risk Index (CRI = PS × D × TM), grounded in biomechanical loading theory and aligned with ISO 11226, ISO 11228-1, and ISO 45001. Expert panel review yielded an S-CVI/Ave of 0.95, indicating strong content validity. Duration–CRI associations were very strong for under-vehicle servicing (ρ = 0.910), tyre fitment (ρ = 0.961), and brake/suspension repair (ρ = 0.945), all p < 0.001. Because duration enters the CRI equation directly and also determines the TM, these correlations are mathematically expected; they show that the index behaves as designed but are not independent evidence of construct validity. Inter-rater reliability across three observers was excellent (ICC = 0.975–0.997), with moderate-to-perfect categorical agreement (weighted κ = 0.557–1.000). Task-level profiling identified tyre demounting, wheel alignment, and drain plug loosening as dominant ergonomic hotspots. These findings provide preliminary support for MIERAT as a content-valid and reliable tool for profiling cumulative postural exposure and planning ergonomic interventions in South African automotive workshops. Validation against independent outcomes, such as musculoskeletal symptoms, fatigue, biomechanical loading, or injury data, is needed to establish its construct and predictive validity.

items.title: Development of occupational health and safety multimedia to enhance learning interest in vocational automotive education
items.abstract: This study aimed to develop automotive occupational health and safety learning multimedia and examine changes in students’ learning interest after its use. The study employed a research and development approach using the ADDIE model and a one-group pretest–posttest design involving 31 Grade 10 automotive engineering students. Data were collected using a 20-item learning interest questionnaire. Expert validation results indicated that the multimedia was highly feasible, with scores exceeding 87%. All questionnaire items were valid, with Cronbach’s alpha values of 0.890 for the pretest and 0.843 for the posttest. The mean learning interest score increased from 70.03 to 86.61, with a normalized gain of 55.52%, categorized as moderate. A one-sample t-test showed that the posttest mean was significantly higher than the reference value of 70 (p < 0.001). These findings suggest that the multimedia has potential to support students’ learning interest. However, the absence of a control group limits causal conclusions.

items.title: Digital Competency and Artificial Intelligence Integration in Modern Administration: Current Demands, Gaps, and Strategic Pathways
items.abstract: Modern administrative governance is undergoing a systemic socio-technical reconfiguration, transitioning rapidly from manual, paper-bound ledgers and legacy e-governance architectures to integrated digital public infrastructure and Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) co-pilot environments. This evolution demands an expanded conceptualization of workforce digital readiness. Grounded in the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), this study systematically examines the operational demands, capacity deficits, and governance challenges confronting administrative personnel across public sector and higher education institutions, particularly within resource-constrained regional environments. Evaluating an integrated dual-layer competency framework—encompassing core computing proficiencies (advanced spreadsheet manipulation, relational database taxonomy, cloud-based records management, and virtual collaboration) alongside emerging Generative AI capabilities (contextual prompt engineering, automated text summarization, cross-linguistic translation, and critical output verification across platforms such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Copilot)—this paper articulates the comparative operational advantages and structural friction points defining modern public administration. Systemic capacity gaps are identified, including technological anxiety, shallow digital literacy, cybersecurity hygiene vulnerabilities, acute geographical infrastructure disparities (exemplified by power grid instability and bandwidth limitations in regional campus settings), and administrative risks surrounding AI hallucinations and data privacy. To bridge the divide between top-down digital governance policies and ground-level workplace execution, we articulate a multi-tiered strategic roadmap incorporating task-oriented contextual training, robust institutional AI governance frameworks, peer-mentorship coaching networks, and sustained capital infrastructure investments, paired with individual lifelong learning pathways. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that while automated tools and AI engines serve as powerful efficiency enablers, rigorous human oversight, procedural discretion, and ethical boundary-setting remain mandatory to safeguard due process, institutional accountability, and transparent governance.

items.title: Distraction-Related Phenomena in Emergency Department Work: A Systematic Literature Review from a Cognitive Ergonomics Perspective
items.abstract: Background: Emergency departments are cognitively demanding environments where healthcare professionals are frequently exposed to interruptions and other distracting factors that may compromise workflow and patient safety. This systematic review aimed to identify factors that distract healthcare professionals in emergency departments and to synthesise their cognitive, organisational, and patient-safety consequences from a cognitive ergonomics perspective. Methods: A systematic literature review was conducted in PubMed, CINAHL Ultimate, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 statement. Studies meeting predefined eligibility criteria were included. Methodological quality was assessed using design-specific critical appraisal tools, and findings were synthesised using inductive content analysis. Results: Nineteen studies met the predefined eligibility criteria and were included in the synthesis. The most frequently reported distraction-related phenomena included communication-related interruptions, telephone calls, and technological and environmental disturbances, while multitasking and task switching were identified as related work processes or responses to competing demands. Across the studies, distraction-related phenomena were associated with cognitive and workflow consequences, including increased workload, reduced situation awareness, work-related stress, and workflow disruption. Only one of the 19 included studies directly examined task errors, whereas the others identified interruptions during medication-related activities and potential safety concerns without directly measuring medication errors or patient harm. Several studies also identified clinically relevant interruptions associated with information exchange and care coordination, alongside unnecessary or poorly timed interruptions that were perceived as disruptive. Conclusions: Distraction-related phenomena are common features of emergency department work and are associated with cognitive and workflow outcomes. However, direct evidence regarding clinical errors and patient safety outcomes remains limited, and the available findings do not establish a causal relationship between distraction-related phenomena and patient harm. Potential cognitive-ergonomic strategies may focus on reducing avoidable and low-value interruptions while preserving clinically necessary communication that supports information exchange and care coordination; however, their effectiveness requires empirical evaluation.

items.title: Do AI-for-Science Agents Preserve Model Safety?
items.abstract: AI-for-Science agents are increasingly being used for formulating scientific hypotheses, running autonomous experiments, and interpreting evidence. These agents are constructed by integrating a large language model (LLM) into a domain-specific agent harness, which in turn can improve the LLM's scientific capability and enable the model to orchestrate scientific tools. In this work, we ask whether model safety is preserved when an LLM is integrated in an AI-for-Science agent harness. We evaluate five agent harnesses on 50 harmful chemistry requests. Specifically, we study how the safety behavior changes under direct prompting, two simple adversarial prompting strategies, and an adaptive attack. Across four recent GPT variants, our results show that the agent harness can increase harmful compliance even under direct prompting. More critically, we find that adaptive attacks that are largely unsuccessful against the base LLM suddenly become highly successful after the agent harness is introduced. Our results show that the safety behavior of the base LLM is not durable once a harness is introduced. Thus, as AI-for-Science agents become more capable and autonomous, the community needs to evaluate and align the agent using domain-specific safety benchmarks.

items.title: Dynamics of collective creativity in AI art competitions
items.abstract: Abstract Creativity is a fundamental part of cultural evolution, but the mechanisms by which groups produce novelty are notoriously difficult to infer from the historical record. Iterated learning experiments have shown that cultural transmission reliably distorts artifacts toward the inductive biases of learners, but most of this work uses linear chains of human participants, and it is unclear how these dynamics play out in the networked, human-AI systems that increasingly shape cultural production. In this study, we analyze one such system: Artbreeder, which hosts daily “remix parties” in which users iteratively build on each other's work from a single seed image, producing branching lineages of images co-created by humans and generative AI. Using 130,882 images from 368 remix parties over 13 months, we find that images become less novel over the course of a party and that each remix step moves less far from its parents, consistent with the stabilization seen in iterated learning experiments, and that late-stage images drift toward the platform's dominant portrait style. More novel “parent” images produce more novel and more complex “children.” More novel children attract more likes but are not remixed more, whereas more complex children are remixed less. Finally, larger remix parties produce images that are more novel but less complex.

items.title: Effect of Trust in AI on Human AI Relationship among University Students
items.abstract: The study aimed to examine the effect of trust in AI on Human-AI relationship among university students. A cross-sectional survey research design was used. The sample comprised 300 university students (150 males and 150 females) selected through convenient sampling technique. Measures included the General Attitude toward AI Scale (GAAIS) by Schepman and Rodway (32 items, Positive α = .84, Negative α = .73), Short Trust in Automation Scale (S-TIAS) by McGrath et al. (3 items, α = .88), and Experiences in Human-AI Relationships Scale (EHARS) by Yang and Oshio (7 items). Correlation analysis showed that trust in AI was positively correlated with Human-AI relationship. The study contributed to the growing literature on Human-AI relationships by highlighting the role of trust in AI in Human-AI interactions among university students. The findings have important implications for AI literacy, technology acceptance, and the development of educational interventions aimed at fostering healthy and effective Human-AI relationships.

items.title: EFFECTS OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI) ON STUDENT PROBLEM-SOLVING SKILLS
items.abstract: This study determined the effect of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-assisted pedagogy on the problem-solving skills of first-year Bachelor of Secondary Education students enrolled in Mathematics in the Modern World at Urdaneta City University. The study was completed in May 2026 during School Year 2025-2026. Using a quasi-experimental pre-test and post-test non-equivalent group design, the researchers compared the performance of students taught through conventional pedagogy with those who experienced AI-supported instruction. Problem-solving performance was examined using George Pólya's four-step framework: understanding the problem, planning a solution, carrying out the plan, and checking the solution. Initial results showed that both groups had limited problem-solving skills before instruction, especially in planning, execution, and verification. After the intervention, both groups improved; however, students exposed to AI-assisted pedagogy obtained stronger gains, particularly in carrying out the plan and overall problem-solving performance. The paired-samples t-test indicated significant improvement within the experimental group, while the independent-samples t-test showed that the experimental group outperformed the conventional group in selected post-test measures. The findings suggest that AI tools, when used with teacher guidance and structured problem-solving activities, can support mathematical learning by offering immediate feedback, alternative explanations, and opportunities for solution checking. The study further indicates that AI should be integrated as a cognitive support rather than as a substitute for independent reasoning.

items.title: Enhancing Cognitive Ergonomics in Robotic Surgery—A Narrative Review
items.abstract: Robotic-assisted surgery (RAS) has transformed minimally invasive procedures by improving physical ergonomics, surgical field visualisation and instrument manipulation. However, RAS introduces unique cognitive load for the surgeon. Cognitive ergonomics aims to enhance the mental resources to optimise the interactions between surgeons and their environment, thereby improving the wellbeing and performance of surgeons and patient outcomes. Current evidence highlights that RAS redistributes, rather than eliminates, ergonomic burden from the physical to the mental domain. Subjective measurement tools remain the most widely used; however, physiological measures offer continuous and real-time data regarding cognitive workload fluctuations during surgery. Strategies to improve cognitive ergonomics include surgeon-level strategies, interface and system design alterations, operating room workflow optimisation, incorporation of artificial intelligence, and training and education. This narrative review summarises the current evidence regarding the mental demands associated with RAS, cognitive workload measures, the consequences of poor cognition, and emerging strategies to improve cognitive ergonomics in RAS.

items.title: Estereotipos Algorítmicos: Un Estudio Experimental sobre Sesgos de Género en la IA Generative
items.abstract: This study analyzes how citizens identify gender biases in narratives generated by artificial intelligence (AI), using ChatGPT as a case study. An online experiment was conducted with 614 Spanish participants, randomly assigned to three conditions: a professional success narrative featuring a female protagonist, a narrative featuring a male protagonist, and a neutral narrative. After exposure, gender bias detection in the story, perceived bias in ChatGPT, and the intention to reduce or correct algorithmic biases were measured. The results show that the narrative featuring a female protagonist was associated with higher bias detection and greater attribution of partiality to ChatGPT. No significant differences were observed according to participants’ gender or educational level. Likewise, indicators of proximity to AI, such as interest in these technologies and the use of AI-based applications, were associated with lower perceived bias in the tool. The findings underscore the need to promote critical AI literacy that helps citizens more critically recognize when its outputs reproduce gender stereotypes or inequalities.

items.title: Evaluating Locally Grounded Generative AI for Health-Policy Support: A Multilevel Mixed-Methods Pilot Study
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may assist evidence-informed health-policy work, but favorable user perceptions and well-written outputs do not establish factual reliability or implementation readiness. A multilevel mixed-methods pilot evaluation examined MUSYA AI, a locally grounded policy-support platform in Thailand. Thirty-five health-sector personnel completed questionnaires, seven participated in Think-Aloud observation, sixteen Policy Briefs were assessed using an expert rubric, and seventy factual claims underwent evidence auditing. The document comparison included eight MUSYA AI and eight ChatGPT (GPT-5.6, OpenAI) outputs under common task instructions and system-specific information access. Mean System Usability Scale, perceived usefulness, and trust scores were 97.29/100, 4.70/5, and 4.57/5, respectively. Ceiling effects and limited internal consistency constrained interpretation of these descriptive indices; user experience, ease of use, and behavioral intention were interpreted at the item level. Observations documented reading and editing, but successful error detection and correction were not evaluated. MUSYA AI documents received higher overall quality ratings than comparator documents (95.38 ± 2.39 versus 72.25 ± 11.90; difference, 23.13 points; bootstrap 95% confidence interval, 15.63–31.38; Hedges’ g = 2.55). However, classification–rationale inconsistencies affected forty-five claims (64.3%), leaving comparative factual-accuracy findings provisional. The small, nonrandomized document sample and absence of verified task pairing prevented causal attribution of quality differences. MUSYA AI elicited favorable pilot-user perceptions and produced higher-rated documents within the evaluated sample. These findings support continued supervised evaluation; institutional readiness requires traceable claim adjudication, demonstrated oversight effectiveness, and broader controlled assessment.

items.title: Evaluating the effectiveness of AI-Based adaptive learning for reading development and self-regulated learning among pupils with dyslexia in Abuja, Nigeria
items.abstract: Children with dyslexia often experience persistent challenges in reading, motivation, and self-regulation within traditional classroom settings that rely on uniform instructional approaches. With the growing integration of artificial intelligence in education, AI-based adaptive learning systems have emerged as innovative tools capable of personalizing instruction and supporting diverse learning needs. This study investigated the effect of AI-based adaptive learning systems on reading performance, motivation, and self-regulation among primary school students with dyslexia in Abuja, Nigeria. A quasi-experimental pretest–posttest control group design was adopted, with a sample of 60 Primary 5 pupils drawn from selected inclusive and special education schools in the Abuja Municipal Area. Data were collected using a Reading Performance Test, Motivation toward Reading Scale, and Self-Regulation in Reading Questionnaire, and analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics, including independent samples t-test. Findings revealed that students exposed to AI-based adaptive learning demonstrated significantly higher improvements across all variables compared to those receiving conventional instruction. The experimental group recorded substantial gains in reading performance (mean gain = 24.20), motivation (mean gain = 1.50), and self-regulation (mean gain = 1.60), compared to the control group. Statistical analysis confirmed that these differences were significant (p < 0.05). These findings align with Cognitive Load Theory, Self-Determination Theory, and Vygotsky’s Zone of Proximal Development. The study concludes that AI-based adaptive learning systems offer an effective approach for improving both academic and psychological outcomes among students with dyslexia. It recommends the integration of AI-driven instructional tools in primary education, alongside teacher training and policy support, to promote inclusive, personalized, and effective learning environments.

items.title: Explainable AI and Real-Time Decisioning for Automated Government Case Management in Saudi Arabia
items.abstract: Automated government case management is moving from digitised workflow toward intelligent triage, eligibility assessment, risk prioritisation and service routing. In Saudi Arabia, this transition is especially consequential because digital government programmes increasingly connect high-volume public services with data-intensive decision processes. The central challenge is not simply whether artificial intelligence can accelerate case handling, but whether decisions can remain timely, reviewable, understandable and contestable when models operate at operational speed. This review examines how explainable artificial intelligence and real-time decisioning can be combined for automated government case management in Saudi Arabia. It synthesises thirty DOI-verified studies published from 2020 to 2025 across explainability, human-AI decision support, public-sector algorithmic governance, Saudi digital government and streaming analytics. The review develops a socio-technical framework in which case intake, data quality, machine reasoning, rule validation, explanation generation, human oversight, notification, appeal and continuous monitoring form one auditable decision loop. The analysis finds that explainability is valuable only when it is matched to the decision recipient and linked to operational controls; generic feature-attribution displays alone do not guarantee justified or trustworthy outcomes. Real-time systems also require explicit latency budgets, uncertainty handling, concept-drift monitoring and escalation rules so that speed does not suppress due process. For Saudi public agencies, successful adoption depends on combining interoperable data, secure governance, accountable ownership and Arabic-capable explanation interfaces with measurable human override and appeal mechanisms. The study proposes evaluation criteria spanning predictive validity, explanation fidelity, decision latency, fairness, reviewability and institutional accountability. It concludes that explainable real-time case management should be designed as governed decision infrastructure rather than as an isolated prediction model.

items.title: Explainable AI in Neural Poetry Generation: Beyond Attention
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) is increasingly important for ensuring transparency and trust in neural systems; however, its applicability to creative text generation remains limited. Neural poetry generation models produce linguistically coherent and stylistically rich outputs, yet explaining decisions such as metaphor construction, emotional tone, and thematic development remains unresolved. This systematic literature review synthesizes 26 peer‐reviewed studies published between 2015 and 2026, following PRISMA 2020 guidelines and a predefined protocol across four major digital libraries. The analysis identifies a fundamental mismatch between existing XAI paradigms and the properties of generative modeling. We propose a taxonomy distinguishing classification‐native methods from generation‐compatible approaches, highlighting their differing assumptions. Based on established criteria of contrastivity, selectivity, and faithfulness, we show that attention mechanisms lack causal validity as explanatory tools. To consolidate these findings, we introduce a unified failure framework comprising five interacting structural limitations: token–semantic mismatch, attention non‐causality, classification–generation incompatibility, evaluation collapse, and human–model ontological misalignment. These limitations collectively constrain the effectiveness of current XAI methods in creative contexts. Our findings indicate that advancing explainability in neural poetry generation requires a shift toward semantic‐level representations, causal intervention‐based approaches, and human‐centered evaluation frameworks that incorporate aesthetic and interpretive dimensions.

items.title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Improving Transparency and Reliability in Automated Decision-Making Systems
items.abstract: Automated decision-making systems increasingly influence healthcare, finance, recruitment, education, public administration, and digital platforms. Although advanced machine-learning models can discover complex relationships, their opaque reasoning can obstruct auditing, contestability, and safe deployment. This narrative review examines how explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) may improve transparency and reliability by clarifying model behavior, revealing data dependencies, supporting error detection, and enabling informed human oversight. It synthesizes established work on interpretable modeling, local feature attribution, surrogate explanations, counterfactual reasoning, explanation evaluation, and governance. A conceptual assurance framework connects data provenance, predictive validation, explanation fidelity, subgroup analysis, and operational monitoring. The paper distinguishes understandable explanations from evidence that a system is accurate, robust, or fair: an attractive explanation alone does not establish reliability. A non-empirical diagram illustrates complementary assurance dimensions without implying measured results. Practical implications include tailoring explanations to decision recipients, testing explanation stability under perturbations, documenting uncertainty, and establishing appeal mechanisms. The review concludes that XAI is most effective when embedded within a wider socio-technical accountability process rather than deployed as a stand-alone visualization technique.

items.title: Fear-Specific Technophobia as a Mediator Between Daily Technical Support and Instrumental Versus Hedonic Technology Use in Later Life: Cross-Sectional Survey Study
items.abstract: Abstract Background Population aging and rapid digitalization have intensified concerns about older adults’ digital participation. Although access disparities have narrowed, older adults continue to differ from younger groups in how they use digital technologies, with their use skewed toward instrumental rather than hedonic purposes. Technophobia is a salient psychological barrier; yet, its distinct fear dimensions and their links to different forms of technology use remain insufficiently differentiated. Daily technical support (DTS) may provide an important sociotechnical context for understanding these relationships. Objective This study aimed to test how DTS promotes older adults’ instrumental and hedonic technology use by reducing multidimensional technophobia (fear of inconvenience, fear of personal failure, and human-machine ambiguity) and whether these mechanisms differ by gender. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted among Chinese adults aged ≥55 years recruited via online platforms and offline communities in Nanjing (June-October 2024). A total of 212 valid responses were included (mean age 66.96, SD 6.96, range 55‐86 years; 142/212, 68.4% women). Measures assessed day-to-day technical support, 3 dimensions of technophobia, instrumental versus hedonic technology use, and demographic variables. We used partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with 5000 bootstrap resamples to test direct, indirect, and moderated mediation effects, reporting 95% bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) CI. Results DTS significantly reduced fear of inconvenience (β=−0.455, 95% BCa CI −0.632 to −0.229; P <.001) but did not significantly affect fear of personal failure ( P =.12) or human-machine ambiguity ( P =.26). Fear of inconvenience and human-machine ambiguity negatively predicted instrumental use (IU; β=−0.215, 95% BCa CI −0.410 to −0.009; P =.05 and β=−0.211, 95% BCa CI −0.389 to −0.001; P =.04). DTS had a positive direct effect on IU (β=0.104, 95% BCa CI 0.009 to 0.203; P =.04) but not on hedonic use (HU; β=0.075; P =.11). The indirect effect of DTS on IU through fear of inconvenience was significant (β=0.097, 95% BCa CI 0.020-0.204). Gender moderated the effect of DTS on fear of inconvenience (β=0.287, 95% BCa CI 0.052-0.518; P =.02), and such conditional indirect effect was significant for men (β=0.098, 95% BCa CI 0.001-0.219) but not for women (β=0.036, 95% BCa CI −0.002 to 0.116). Conclusions DTS was associated with greater instrumental technology use among older adults through lower fear of inconvenience, with a stronger indirect association among men, whereas no comparable pathway emerged for HU. This suggests that gender may shape how older adults benefit psychologically from technical support rather than reflect general differences in support needs. Interventions should move beyond one-size-fits-all approaches by providing targeted, task-oriented support that addresses older adults’ specific technological fears and practical barriers.

items.title: From Automation to Augmentation: Artificial Intelligence, Competence Evolution, and Career Sustainability in the Accounting Profession
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the content of accounting work, but the career consequences of that change remain less clear in emerging economies. Using field responses from 600 accounting and finance professionals in Nigeria, Ghana, and Kenya (200 per country), this paper examines whether intensive AI use is associated with professional role transformation, whether role transformation is associated with competence evolution, and whether those evolving competencies are linked to career sustainability. Learning and organizational support is considered both as a contextual resource and as a potential moderator. The analysis uses multi-item composite measures, HC3-robust path regressions, 5,000-resample bootstrapping, effect-size estimates, 10-fold cross-validation, and exploratory country comparisons. AI adoption was positively associated with role transformation (β = .491, p < .001). AI adoption (β = .286, p < .001) and role transformation (β = .462, p < .001) jointly explained 42.6% of the variance in competence evolution, while competence evolution was positively associated with career sustainability (β = .414, p < .001). The direct role-transformation effect on career sustainability was negligible (β = .013, p = .764), whereas the indirect effect through competence evolution was significant (β = .192, 95% bootstrap CI [.146, .242]). The serial pathway from AI adoption through role transformation and competence evolution to career sustainability was also significant (β = .094, 95% CI [.069, .123]). Learning and organizational support had a positive main effect but did not moderate the competence-sustainability relationship. The results suggest that the long-term value of AI-related role change depends less on the fact that work changes than on whether professionals acquire the digital, analytical, advisory, and ethical capabilities needed to succeed in the redesigned role. items.title: From Instrument to Economic Actor: Generative and Agentic AI as a New Logic of Business Model Innovation
items.abstract: (1) Background: Generative and, increasingly, agentic artificial intelligence (AI) are reshaping how firms create, deliver, and capture value. Yet business model innovation (BMI) research often assumes that humans retain design authority while digital technologies support analysis or execute predefined decisions. This assumption becomes contestable when AI systems can generate value-bearing artifacts, participate in organizational decision-making, and undertake goal-directed action within delegated boundaries. (2) Approach: Integrating business-model and activity-system research, dynamic capabilities, socio-technical and human–AI decision-making perspectives, and research on generative and agentic AI, this concept paper develops a framework that distinguishes three logics of AI-enabled BMI: a supporting logic (AI as instrument), a generative logic (AI as co-creator), and an agentic logic (AI as delegated economic actor). The framework distinguishes business-model operation from business-model innovation and identifies delegated reconfiguration authority as a key condition under which agentic action can constitute BMI. (3) Contribution: The paper advances six propositions explaining how AI redistributes ideation, decision, execution, and reconfiguration rights; how machine agency may compress the interval between business-model reconfigurations; how value-capture mechanisms may change; and why complementary capabilities, governance, and legitimacy remain decisive. (4) Conclusions: The paper offers a focused research agenda centered on agency allocation and decision rights, the temporal dynamics and measurement of BMI, and value capture and governance in agent-mediated business models. It thereby provides a more precise theoretical basis for distinguishing autonomous operation within a business model from autonomous or semi-autonomous reconfiguration of the business model itself.

items.title: From Natural Equality to Constitutional Legitimacy: Locke’s Political Anthropology and Algorithmic Governance
items.abstract: The growing integration of artificial intelligence into governance challenges the conditions under which political authority can be considered legitimate. Algorithmic systems increasingly mediate decisions that shape citizens’ lives, yet their operations frequently bypass human judgment and obscure the justificatory basis of political authority. This article reinterprets John Locke’s political philosophy as a normative framework for assessing algorithmic authority. By reconstructing Locke’s account of reason, equality, consent, and fiduciary trust, it brings his political anthropology into dialogue with contemporary debates on algorithmic accountability and digital constitutionalism. The article argues that AI governance does not merely raise technical or regulatory problems; it threatens the conditions under which citizens can understand, evaluate, and contest the exercise of power. Because many AI systems operate through models that neither officials nor citizens can meaningfully interpret, they generate forms of automated prerogative that weaken the fiduciary relationship between governors and governed. Against this danger, the article advances a Lockean criterion for computational governance: algorithmic authority can be considered legitimate only insofar as it preserves intelligibility, fiduciary accountability, and contestability. Legitimacy cannot be restored through technical adjustment alone; it requires institutional conditions under which power remains publicly intelligible, politically answerable, and open to challenge by those subject to it.

items.title: From Responsible Leadership to Responsible AI Governance: A Leadership-Based Framework for AI Governance in Organizations
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping organizational decision-making, managerial roles, and accountability, yet responsible AI governance remains dominated by principles, technical controls, and regulatory compliance. This conceptual paper develops a human leadership-based framework for translating responsible AI principles into organizational governance. In the framework, the responsible leader is an accountable human organizational actor—such as a board member, senior executive, business leader, or designated decision owner—while AI is treated as a governed technological system or operational agent rather than the accountable leader. Human responsible leadership influences responsible AI governance (RAIG) capability through six mediating organizational processes: stakeholder orientation, ethical sensemaking, accountability architecture, meaningful human oversight, inclusive participation, and long-term value orientation. RAIG capability is defined as the higher-order organizational capacity to institutionalize and adapt lifecycle governance arrangements; it enables observable governance practices, which are conceptually separated from downstream responsible AI outcomes. AI operational autonomy is proposed as a focal moderator: the leadership-to-RAIG pathway should become stronger when AI can initiate or execute consequential actions with limited contemporaneous human approval, particularly where actions are difficult to reverse, trace, or interrupt. The framework offers testable propositions and a research agenda, but it is conceptual and requires empirical validation; it is not a technical safety guarantee.

items.title: Generative AI in Second Language Video Composing: Investigating Students' Critical Digital Literacies and Multimodal Redesign
items.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in digital multimodal composing (DMC) presents both opportunities and challenges for second language (L2) research and pedagogy. While GenAI tools provide linguistic and multimodal support, they also raise concerns about biased information, culturally generic outputs, and technological overreliance. This qualitative study investigates L2 students' enactment of critical digital literacies (CDL) during GenAI‐assisted video composing. Drawing on CDL as a theoretical orientation and the analytical heuristic of critical awareness, critical identities, critical relationships, and critical actions, the study examines how students negotiated and revised AI‐generated video representations. Using multimodal critical discourse analysis of screen recordings, final video artifacts, focus group interviews, and reflective essays from 20 L2 students, the findings reveal four interrelated forms of CDL enactment. Students demonstrated critical awareness of GenAI's culturally limited outputs, authored critical identities through multimodal redesign, negotiated critical relationships with peers and GenAI, and engaged in localized critical action against cultural erasure. However, students' varied responses also highlight the uneven opportunities for CDL enactment across student groups. These findings offer theoretical and pedagogical implications for supporting L2 learners' critical engagement with algorithmic assumptions, cultural biases, and multimodal representations in GenAI‐assisted DMC.

items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and the Formation of Future Communication Professionals- Student Perceptions, Semiotic Mediation and Educational Challenges
items.abstract: The growing presence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in universities is transforming how academic knowledge is accessed, interpreted, and processed by students. Students increasingly rely on AI-based systems to retrieve information, summarize large volumes of content, clarify complex concepts and support academic writing. While these tools can improve speed, accessibility and day-to-day study support, they also raise difficult questions about intellectual autonomy, authorship, evaluation and the cultivation of critical reasoning. This paper explores the educational and professional implications of GenAI for future communication specialists. The study combines a qualitative exploratory investigation of student perceptions with a narrative literature review of recent academic work on AI in higher education. The empirical component was conducted with 20 undergraduate students enrolled in communication-related and engineering programs at the University of Medicine, Pharmacy, Sciences and Technology “George Emil Palade” in Târgu Mureș. Data were collected through semi-structured questions and analyzed through an inductive thematic coding procedure. The findings indicate that students perceive GenAI primarily as a practical learning assistant capable of translating dense academic content into more accessible explanations. At the same time, they express concerns regarding dependency, superficial learning, weakened independent effort and the authenticity of assessment. The paper argues that GenAI should not be treated as a substitute for human cognition, but as a mediated and reflexive instrument that can support intellectual formation when used transparently, critically and ethically. For communication education, this means preparing students not only to operate AI tools effectively, but also to question their outputs, interpret their symbolic effects and integrate them responsibly within professional communication practice.
